summary:
Rescue Force developed by Team Megatron, is a satellite-powered humanitarian platform designed to help rescue teams, recovery organizations, researchers, decision-makers, and the public understand war-related surface changes and their impact on communities.

Built for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Dancing with the SARs,” Rescue Force combines NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations with supporting geospatial data to identify potential changes in conflict-affected areas.

The platform features an interactive 3D/2D map, satellite observation timeline, potential damage indicators, population density visualization, incident prioritization, and humanitarian decision-support tools. It integrates information from sources such as Sentinel-1, NASA FIRMS, NASA Black Marble, OpenStreetMap, and WorldPop.

Rescue Force emphasizes evidence transparency, uncertainty, and human verification rather than presenting satellite observations as confirmed damage. Its public demonstration uses clearly labelled sample data, while the project documents radar-processing methods for the South Lebanon study area.

Our mission is to transform complex satellite information into accessible insights that support humanitarian assessment, recovery planning, and a better understanding of war-affected communities.
details:
Project Details — Rescue Force | Team Megatron

Rescue Force is a satellite-powered humanitarian intelligence and decision-support platform developed by Team Megatron for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Dancing with the SARs.” Our project focuses on monitoring war-affected areas, identifying potential changes in civilian infrastructure, and supporting humanitarian assessment and post-conflict recovery.

What Does Rescue Force Do?

Rescue Force transforms complex satellite observations and geospatial information into an accessible, interactive experience. Our study focuses on South Lebanon, where conflict-related damage, disrupted infrastructure, and limited ground access can make humanitarian assessments challenging.

Using NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations, our analytical approach compares satellite acquisitions from different dates to identify unusual surface changes. We examine radar backscatter and polarization changes and use an Isolation Forest machine-learning approach to identify potential change candidates. Supporting datasets provide additional context, helping users understand possible impacts on buildings, infrastructure, and communities.

The platform provides:

  • Interactive 3D, 2D, and split-view maps to explore affected areas and geographic context.
  • Satellite observation timelines to understand available acquisition dates and monitoring gaps, with historical before-and-after comparison and playback as planned extensions.
  • Potential damage indicators to investigate areas requiring further assessment.
  • Population density visualization to understand historical population distribution and potential civilian exposure.
  • Incident prioritization using transparent ranking factors and uncertainty ranges.
  • Humanitarian decision support through suggested checks, infrastructure context, recovery planning indicators, and evidence gaps.
  • Data transparency through observation dates, source information, and evidence classifications.

Our public demonstration uses clearly labelled sample data to illustrate these capabilities. It is not presented as a live, verified humanitarian assessment system.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Rescue Force aims to make satellite-based information more understandable and useful for rescue teams, humanitarian organizations, government agencies, recovery planners, researchers, and the public.

By combining remote sensing with geographic and population context, the platform can help users identify locations that may need further investigation, understand the possible scale of civilian infrastructure impacts, and support more informed recovery planning.

Our long-term goal is to make war-related surface changes and recovery patterns easier to visualize across different satellite observation dates, supporting evidence-based decisions while reducing dependence on immediate physical access to affected locations.

Technologies, Tools, and Data Sources

We developed Rescue Force using a modern geospatial web architecture:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, and CesiumJS for interactive geographic visualization.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI for application services and data integration.
  • Database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS for spatial information management.
  • Satellite processing and machine learning: Python-based radar analysis and Isolation Forest for identifying unusual surface-change patterns.
  • Development and collaboration: Git and GitHub for source control and collaborative development.

Our data sources include NASA–ISRO NISAR, Sentinel-1 radar observations, NASA FIRMS active-fire information, NASA Black Marble nighttime-light observations, OpenStreetMap geographic features, WorldPop population estimates, and supporting building and terrain datasets.

What Makes Rescue Force Creative?

Rescue Force goes beyond displaying satellite imagery. It connects potential radar-detected changes with the human consequences that humanitarian responders and recovery planners need to consider.

Its innovation lies in integrating satellite change indicators, population information, infrastructure context, incident prioritization, and decision-support tools into one interactive environment.

Instead of presenting uncertain satellite measurements as confirmed destruction, Rescue Force communicates what has been observed, what may have changed, and what still requires verification.

This approach helps bridge the gap between scientific Earth observation and practical humanitarian understanding.

Challenges and Responsible Design Considerations

Our team considered several important limitations while developing the project.

NISAR observations are acquired periodically, not continuously, so satellite monitoring cannot provide an uninterrupted real-time view. Radar changes may result from multiple physical causes and cannot independently confirm conflict damage.

Population estimates may reflect historical conditions rather than current displacement or occupancy. Nighttime-light changes do not necessarily prove electricity outages, and potential road or shelter conditions cannot be verified from satellite observations alone.

To address these challenges, Rescue Force emphasizes uncertainty ranges, evidence classification, source transparency, and human verification. Missing information is treated as unknown rather than assumed to indicate no damage.

Our vision is to turn complex Earth observation data into accessible humanitarian insights, helping people better understand the changing geography of conflict and supporting informed, responsible recovery planning.
